title: Radiators and Interior
premise: Bridge inspector Beatrix Quintana has spent her life translating instability into load ratings, but at her mother's funeral a stranger calls the family by the surname 'Vasquez'—a name her father forbade decades ago. Digging through her mother's sealed letters, Beatrix discovers the family's true identity was buried alongside a betrayal: her father took another man's name, inheritance, and history, and her mother spent forty years as his silent accomplice. As the stranger—now an elderly man claiming to be the dispossessed Vasquez heir—presses his claim before the estate closes, Beatrix must decide whether loyalty to the dead father she loved outweighs the truth her mother finally trusted her to carry. She ends by testifying to the truth, surrendering the house, and renaming herself with both names, finding belonging not in the family she defended but in the one she finally tells honestly.
about_author: Coral Eastwick is a former structural engineer from the Pacific Northwest whose novels examine the load-bearing secrets of ordinary families. She writes from a converted ferry cabin, where she keeps her late mother's unlabeled photograph albums within reach.

chapters.title: Expansion Joints
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, inspects a aging truss bridge the week of her mother's funeral, measuring cracks with the same detached precision she applies to her own grief. At the graveside, a weathered stranger named Elias murmurs the name 'Vasquez,' watching her family like a man confirming an address. Beat: the first hairline fracture in a structure she thought sound.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, catalogs her mother's belongings and finds a locked tin beneath floorboard radiators—her mother's habit of hiding warmth in plain sight. Inside: letters addressed to 'Mrs. Vasquez,' unopened, dated across forty years. Her brother Daniel insists on burning them as 'mom's clutter.' Beat: dread sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: A Man by the Wrong Name
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He waits outside Beatrix's office, an old man with a court summons and a photograph of two boys—one her father, one himself. He explains, haltingly, that his family's name and property were taken in 1962, and that Beatrix's mother wrote to him once a year, apologizing. Beat: the ground tilting; Beatrix's father becomes a stranger.

chapters.title: Load Rating
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, cross-examines her uncle Ray, the family's keeper of official memory, who deflects with jokes and warns her that some bridges are better condemned than repaired. Daniel, furious, accuses her of disgracing Dad's memory for a con man's lawsuit. Beat: loyalty hardening into a wall she can feel herself standing behind.

chapters.title: What Mother Kept Warm
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, deciphers the letters: her mother's yearly confessions, her father's escalating fear, and one final sealed envelope marked 'For Beatrix, when you're ready to be angry with me.' Inside, her mother admits she knew everything from the wedding day and chose the family over the truth. Beat: grief complicated by a terrible, intimate understanding.

chapters.title: The Vasquez Heir
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. His deposition approaches, but his granddaughter urges him to drop it—he's chasing a dead man's name at the cost of his last years. He reveals to Beatrix that he doesn't want the house; he wants his father's grave moved off land registered to a stranger. Beat: the moral stakes shrink to something human, and harder to refuse.

chapters.title: Family Arranged Around a Question
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, convenes Daniel, Uncle Ray, and her aunt to settle it privately before court. Daniel offers Elias money; Ray offers silence; Beatrix realizes the whole family's architecture—every tradition, every taboo—was load-bearing for this one secret. Beat: rising tension; she understands she must testify or become her father.

chapters.title: Condemned
chapters.summary: Elias's POV, on the courthouse steps the night before the hearing, he nearly walks away—until Beatrix arrives unannounced and asks him to tell her everything, not the court. He recounts the theft in full: her father was the farmhand who became the son when the real heir was sent away. Beat: the climax's fuse lit; Beatrix chooses truth over tribe.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, takes the stand, presents her mother's letters, and confirms the name change and the theft, against Daniel's pleading eyes. The estate is settled; the house and the grave plot go to Elias. Daniel cuts her off outside the courthouse. Beat: climax—devastating, clean, and irreversible.

chapters.title: Two Names
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV, months later, inspects the old bridge one final time before its scheduled demolition, then helps Elias plant a marker at his father's restored grave. She legally adds Vasquez to her name—not as inheritance, but as acknowledgment—and writes her first letter to Daniel, unsent but sincere. Beat: belonging rebuilt on truth; the structure, though condemned, finally holds.
